summary:
We have developed LunaNav, a visual, interactive web application designed to support the planning and comparison of candidate landing sites near the lunar South Pole.
How it addresses the challenge:
South Pole missions face severe lighting and communication constraints due to low solar angles and long shadows cast by crater rims and ridges. Moving away from complex, specialized interfaces and fragmented datasets, LunaNav integrates lunar terrain elevation models with solar and Earth ephemeris calculations into a single, intuitive platform. Users can identify candidate sites, browse timelines to visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the true local horizon, and compare multiple locations and dates side-by-side.
Why it matters:
LunaNav accelerates early-stage decision-making for mission planners and engineers by providing immediate assessments of potential sunlight exposure and direct-to-Earth visibility windows. It also lowers technical barriers, enabling educators, students, and the general public to interactively explore and understand the trade-offs involved in lunar exploration.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

LunaNav   is an interactive, browser-based visual decision-support platform designed to evaluate and compare candidate landing sites near the Moon’s south pole.

• Site & Time Selection: Users select a candidate landing site (such as Shackleton Crater Rim or Malapert Massif) and choose a specific date or mission timeframe using an interactive timeline scrubber.

• Terrain-Aware Horizon Simulation: The application computes a 360-degree local terrain horizon profile from lunar elevation datasets and overlays the real-time azimuth and elevation paths of both the Sun and Earth.

• Visibility & Comparison Engine: By comparing celestial elevation angles against the local terrain horizon, LunaNav distinguishes between ideal geometric visibility and actual unobstructed line-of-sight. Users can compare multiple landing sites or dates side-by-side to evaluate potential sunlight duration and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows.

2. Benefits

• Unified Situational Awareness: Eliminates the need to mentally combine fragmented astronomical tables and topographic maps by merging illumination, Earth visibility, and terrain obstruction into one visual workspace.

• Rapid Trade-Off Analysis: Allows mission planners and engineers to screen and compare multiple candidate sites under consistent assumptions in seconds rather than hours.

• Dual-Mode Accessibility: Features a simplified educational view with intuitive indicators for students and the public, alongside an engineering view exposing precise azimuth/elevation telemetry and data exports.

 3. Expected Impact

• Accelerating Early Mission Planning: Provides aerospace researchers, rover teams, and mission designers with a fast, transparent preliminary screening tool for polar lunar operations.

• Democratizing Space Science (STEM): Empowers educators, students, and the general public to actively explore the real engineering challenges behind NASA’s Artemis program and lunar exploration without needing specialized command-line software.

 4. Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware & Software Used

 • Data Sources & Ephemeris: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO LOLA) Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for lunar topography, paired with NAIF SPICE kernels and JPL Horizons data for planetary positions.

• Backend & Scientific Computation: Python (utilizing SpiceyPy, Astropy, and NumPy) to transform coordinate frames, calculate local azimuth/elevation angles, and pre-compute 360-degree horizon profiles into lightweight JSON datasets.

• Frontend & Visualization: JavaScript / TypeScript, React, and Three.js / WebGL (alongside HTML5/CSS3) to render interactive 3D/2D horizon plots, dynamic timelines, and side-by-side comparison dashboards.

• Hardware & Collaboration Software: Standard developer laptops, cloud hosting (Vercel / GitHub Pages) for instant web deployment, Git/GitHub for version control, and Figma for UI/UX wireframing.

   5. Creative Aspects

• Visualizing "Hidden" Obstructions: Rather than displaying abstract numerical coordinates, LunaNav places the user directly on the lunar surface with a 360-degree panoramic horizon view, making low-angle polar shadows and Earth-blocking crater rims immediately intuitive.

• Transparent Uncertainty Communication: Instead of giving an opaque "best site" score, LunaNav creatively separates "above ideal horizon" from "clear of local terrain" using clear visual states and timelines, teaching users why a site works or fails.

 6. Team Considerations & Design Factors

• Scientific Integrity vs. False Precision: Our team prioritized responsible communication by clearly labeling outputs as potential sunlight and potential direct-to-Earth line of sight, explicitly noting terrain resolution limits and unmodeled factors (such as antenna link-budgets or solar panel efficiency).

• Performance & Accessibility: To ensure smooth performance on standard school laptops and tablets without heavy GPU loads, we pre-computed horizon elevation profiles and used color-blind-friendly visual palettes.
